clusters.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
clusters.neutral_headline: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter

items.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
items.standfirst: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James CaponYour report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place (BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November).The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

items.title: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter
items.standfirst: The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline MitchellThe news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians (NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November)Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system. items.title: Anti-vaccine group once led by RFK Jr back on Facebook and Instagram after being banned
items.standfirst: Children’s Health Defense was removed from Facebook and Instagram in 2022. Meta declined to comment on why it allowed the group backAn anti-vaccine group led for years by Robert F Kennedy Jr has been allowed back on Facebook and Instagram, four years after Meta removed the group for repeatedly violating its misinformation policies.A review by the Guardian found that Children’s Health Defense (CHD) has reopened or opened six accounts on Facebook and Instagram from May through September this year. The group is using its accounts to share false and misleading information about topics including vaccines and deadly measles outbreaks at a time when measles has come roaring back. Health officials have reported 10 measles-associated deaths in the United States this year, and the country this week lost its measles elimination status in an official recognition that it is again endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years. Continue reading...

clusters.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
clusters.neutral_headline: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck

items.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
items.standfirst: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everythingThe skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.”It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”. Continue reading...

items.standfirst: Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safetyA senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety.Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told. Continue reading...
